groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write ONE WORD for each answer.

parts.context: A lecturer outlines the history and future of wearable devices.

transcript.text: Good morning. Today's topic is wearable technology, and I'd like to start with a bit of history, because many people think this is a completely new phenomenon, when in fact its roots go back several decades.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: I should say that the word wearable covers a very wide range of products, from simple pedometers to devices that are implanted under the skin. For this lecture I'll concentrate on the devices that people actually wear on their wrists, because they have the largest market.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: The first mass-market wearable was the calculator watch, which appeared in nineteen seventy-five. Its main purpose was to do simple sums, and it was a fashionable object for a few years. Its major limitation was the tiny keys, which were almost impossible to press accurately.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: Then there was a long gap. The next real breakthrough came in two thousand and nine, when the first popular fitness bands were launched. These were designed to count steps, and users loved seeing their daily total on a small screen.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: During this period, companies spent heavily on research, but the technology was not yet ready. Screens used a lot of power, processors were slow, and there was no easy way to connect a device to the internet, so most prototypes never reached the shops.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: However, early fitness bands had a significant drawback: the battery life was short, often only a couple of days, so people frequently forgot to recharge them and stopped wearing them altogether.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: Today's smartwatches go much further. They can measure heart rate continuously, and some models can detect an irregular rhythm and warn the wearer to see a doctor. Several studies have reported cases in which this early warning saved lives.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: Part of the appeal of these watches is convenience. You do not need to take a phone out of your pocket to check a message or follow a map, and many users say this makes them less distracted, although others feel the opposite.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: Doctors are interested in this data, but they are also cautious. A watch can produce false alarms, which cause unnecessary anxiety, so most doctors treat the information as a starting point for tests rather than a diagnosis.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: There's also the question of privacy. The information collected by these devices is highly personal, and in some countries insurance companies have asked customers to share it in exchange for lower prices.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: This raises difficult legal questions that governments have not yet answered. Who owns the data that your watch produces: you, the manufacturer, or the company that stores it? At present, the answer varies from country to country.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: Looking ahead, researchers are developing devices that don't look like devices at all. Examples include clothing with sensors woven into the fabric, and even contact lenses that measure sugar levels in the body.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: Whatever the future holds, one thing is certain. The devices will become smaller, cheaper and more accurate, and the debate about how they should be used will become more important, not less.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES

transcript.text: So wearable technology is moving from a fashion accessory to a serious health tool. Whether people will accept the privacy trade-offs is something we'll discuss in next week's seminar. Thank you.
transcript.speaker: DR HAYES
